topic.title: Reading Input from the Console
topic.description: Using Scanner class to read user input

sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever wondered how programs talk to users? Today, you'll learn how to read input from the console - like having a conversation with your code!

• How to use the Scanner class to read user input
• Different methods to read numbers, text, and more
• Common mistakes to avoid when reading input

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine the Scanner class like a friendly receptionist at a hotel. When a guest (user) arrives, the receptionist (Scanner) asks for their details and writes them down for you.

The Scanner class helps your program 'listen' to what the user types. Here's how it works:

• First, you create a Scanner object that listens to the keyboard (System.in)
• Then you ask the user for input with a clear prompt
• Finally, you read what they typed using special methods

sections.title: 📊 Visual Simulation
sections.content: Step-by-step visualization of how Reading Input from the Console works:

steps.title: Create the Scanner
steps.description: First, we create a Scanner object that will listen to the keyboard. This is like hiring our receptionist!

steps.title: Ask for Input
steps.description: We show a message to the user telling them what to enter. This is like the receptionist asking for a name.

steps.title: Read the Input
steps.description: The Scanner reads what the user types and stores it in a variable. The user presses Enter when done.

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Always import java.util.Scanner at the top of your file
✓ Create only ONE Scanner object per program (don't make multiple!)
✓ Use clear prompts so users know what to enter
✓ Match the method to the data type (nextInt() for integers, nextDouble() for decimals)
✓ Remember to close the Scanner when done (input.close())

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use print() instead of println() for prompts so the user types on the same line
Check for valid input before using it (we'll learn this soon!)
Give examples in your prompts (e.g., "Enter your height in cm: ")
donts: Don't create multiple Scanner objects for System.in
Don't use nextInt() when you need a decimal number
sections.protip: Always put a space after your prompt (like "Enter age: ") so the user's input doesn't stick to your text!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Reading Input from the Console used in real apps?

examples.how: Reading usernames and passwords when users log in
Reading the amount of money to withdraw or deposit
Reading configuration options when starting programs

problem.description: Create a program that asks for a user's name and age, then prints a message like "Hello [name]! You are [age] years old."
hints: Use nextLine() for the name and nextInt() for the age
Put a space after your prompts so the input looks nice
problem.explanation: We first import Scanner, then create a Scanner object. We use nextLine() for the name (which can contain spaces) and nextInt() for the age. Finally, we print the combined message and close the Scanner.

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Scanner class is your program's way of listening to user input
📌 Always use clear prompts so users know what to enter
📌 Match the method to the data type (nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine())
📌 Practice makes perfect - try reading different types of input!
📌 Ready for next topic: Handling different types of input errors!
